new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive but confined to a two-syllable initial window: every word carries its one contrastive (emic) stress on either the first or the second syllable (minimal pairs 'ata 'bone' vs a'ta 'ear', 'uhijo 'smell' vs u'hijo 'roll', 'samakavo 'I find' vs a'manavo 'I fasten'); further stresses fall rhythmically on every alternate syllable after the contrastive one and are non-contrastive. Per the orthography note (ms p.35) the less frequent patterns are second-syllable stress in disyllables and initial stress in three- and four-syllable words, i.e. disyllables are usually initial-stressed and longer words usually second-syllable-stressed. The 1992 OPD restates: 'Stress is phonemic.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-contrastive rhythmic stress on every alternate syllable after the contrastive stress (5.3.1); in '_ _ _ _ words the predictable third-syllable stress is often heavier than the contrastive first-syllable stress, intensities fluctuate (5.3.2.3, ms p.26); /i'u/ and /u'V/ count as two syllables for stress placement (5.3.3.1-2).
new_statements.exceptions: A few grammatical words consist of two phonological words with two emic stresses, e.g. /'tati?i'ura/ 'bug', /si'u?usi'u?u/ 'early morning' (5.3.3.3, ms p.29); greater tendency for first-syllable stress in four-syllable 'CVV CVV words (5.3.2.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, citation forms from a c.700-word corpus (Numba village speakers). 5.3.4: the emic stress of the phrase-final word is stronger, higher pitched and lengthened, with a general upglide at the end of every pause group in narrative.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Parlier sources describe Managalasi (= Ese, mcq, esee1247) as spoken at Numba village near the Sila airstrip (central Managalasi); Dutton 1969 lists up to eleven Managalasi 'isolects', so the statement is for the Numba variety. SIL PNG catalogues the language as 'Ese [mcq]'.

sources.note: Second-hand. Sec. 5.83.73 (p.145-146): 'J. and J. Parlier show stress to be contrastive on first and second syllables of words.' Sec. 5.82: 'In the three languages of the Family studied in more detail (viz., Koiari, Aomie, and Managalasi) stress has been found to be phonemic.' Also notes Parliers treat [ʉ] as /iu/ with stress on the second vowel.
